title: How Do Incumbents Respond to the Threat of Entry? Evidence from the Major Airlines
research_question: How do incumbent firms respond to a heightened threat of future entry by a competitor, as distinct from their response to actual entry? Specifically, do incumbents preemptively cut prices, expand capacity, or otherwise alter behavior when entry becomes much more likely but has not yet occurred, and are such actions aimed at deterring or accommodating the prospective entrant?
data_description: The core data come from the U.S. Department of Transportation's DB1A files (a 10% sample of all domestic tickets) for 1993:Q1 through 2004:Q4, aggregated to the route-carrier-quarter level, providing average logged fares and total passenger counts on direct flights. Routes are defined by pairs of endpoint airports, restricted to the 59 airports Southwest ever served. Major incumbent carriers analyzed are American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, TWA, United, and US Airways. The sample contains over 19,000 route-carrier-quarter observations covering 704 routes where Southwest's entry was threatened (533 eventually entered). Supplementary capacity data—segment-level passengers, available seats, and flights—come from the DOT's T-100 database, aggregated to route-carrier-quarter (about 3,152 matched observations). Entry timing and announcements were verified using Lexis-Nexis searches of local business press.
institutional_context: The U.S. passenger airline industry following deregulation features Southwest Airlines as a prominent low-cost carrier whose route expansion is highly predictable: once Southwest establishes operations at both endpoint airports of a city-pair, the quarterly probability it begins flying that route jumps roughly seventyfold (to about 18.5%) relative to other routes. Southwest typically announces new airport service months in advance—negotiating gate leases, advertising, and selling tickets—so incumbents and industry insiders learn well before flights commence. This network expansion pattern generates discrete, observable shifts in the likelihood that major incumbents (e.g., American, United, Delta) will face Southwest competition on specific routes, while the airline industry's well-documented sensitivity to airport presence, hub effects, frequent-flyer loyalty, and capacity decisions provides a rich setting in which to study how dominant carriers might react to looming low-cost competition before it materializes.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: EVENT STUDY — treatment = routes with entry threat, control = routes without entry threat; shock/instrument/cutoff = entry announcement

key_variables.treatment: routes where a new competitor announces entry
key_variables.control: routes without any new entry announcements

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Incumbent airlines reduce prices in response to the threat of new competitors entering their routes.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Prices decrease by approximately 15% on threatened routes.
